Over-Defense in Coding Agents Begins at Silent Forks

Hanjun Luo Affiliation: New York University Affiliation: New York University Abu Dhabi    Xuecheng Liu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Xiucheng Zhang Affiliation: New York University    Zhuoning Xu Affiliation: New York University    Yingbin Jin Affiliation: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University    Yankai Chen Affiliation: McGill University Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence    Xue Liu Affiliation: McGill University Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence    Hanan Salam
Abstract

Language models behind coding agents are post-trained with outcome rewards, and recent methods concentrate credit on the turns that decide the outcome. We find that defensive actions beyond what a task requires escape both. They begin at silent forks, the turns where every next action leads to the same outcome. Such actions leave the success rate unchanged, and frontier models take the disproportionate branch there in up to 91% of decisive actions under implicit budgets. The most direct fix, a checker in the trajectory reward, reaches these forks only through fully proportionate trajectories, leaving 74% of GRPO groups with identical rewards and behavior unchanged. This motivates a rethink of where learning signals belong, namely where behavior diverges, which a behavioral checker can locate and the outcome cannot. Our method, ForkDPO, contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action at the same prefix, at silent forks on both sides of the required behavior. On a test set of unseen repositories, it lowers a 4B model’s disproportionate behavior from 70.3% to 58.9%, against 67.7% for DPO at randomly chosen turns, establishing behavioral divergence as a learning signal for how agents act beyond whether they finish. The code is publicly available.11 1 https://github.com/Astarojth/silent-forks

††footnotetext: †Corresponding author: Hanan Salam. Contact: Hanjun Luo, hl6266@nyu.edu.

1 Introduction

Coding agents now resolve repository-level tasks with little human supervision (Jimenez et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025c), and the language models behind them are increasingly post-trained with task success as the reward (Wei et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025). While working on a task, the agent also decides how many defensive actions to take, such as which tests to run, how often to rerun them, and what to check before submitting. Language models often do more than a task needs (Chen et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025), and in coding much of this excess is defensive. For example, agents rerun the same test on unchanged code (Bouzenia and Pradel, 2025). Defensive actions beyond what a task requires are known as over-defense, and even when the task rules such an action out, frontier models take it in 11.2–58.7% of runs (Luo et al., 2026).

Current post-training locates learning signals by the outcome. An outcome reward only tells the model whether the task succeeded, and recent methods go further by concentrating credit on the turns that decide the outcome (Zhang, 2026; Zheng et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). For instance, process verifiers score each step by the change in the chance of success before and after it (Setlur et al., 2025), and tree-search RL branches at the most uncertain tokens and credits each step by how much it raises the success rate (Hou et al., 2025). These methods share the premise that the turns worth learning from are those where the choice changes the outcome, so a turn whose outcome is already settled receives no signal (Lei et al., 2026).

To find where over-defense begins, we replay the commands of successful trajectories with a behavioral checker and mark the first action beyond what the task requires. We find that over-defense begins at forks whose outcome is already settled. Prior work calls a point a fork when resampling there leads to very different outcomes (Bigelow et al., 2025), and over-defense arises in the opposite case. As shown in Figure 1, once the requested test has passed, submitting and running the test again both pass the task oracle. We call such a turn a Silent Fork, one at which the agent’s next actions differ in proportionality while all of them lead to the same outcome. In our experiments, almost every fork where over-defense begins leaves the repository unchanged on both branches, and over-defensive runs succeed as often as the rest. When the instruction leaves the checking budget implicit, four frontier models given the prefixes of these forks take the disproportionate branch in up to 91% of their decisive actions, those that test, check, or submit.

Silent forks explain why outcome signals cannot reach over-defense. Every action at a silent fork has the same value under an outcome reward, so the policy gradient there vanishes. The most direct fix adds the checker to the trajectory reward, much as length-controlled RL penalizes overly long reasoning (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025). Such a signal reaches a fork only through trajectories that are proportionate at every fork, and these become rare as tasks grow longer. We train with this reward using GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), a common outcome-based RL algorithm that learns only from reward differences within a group of rollouts (Yu et al., 2025). In 71% of implicit-budget groups every rollout receives the same reward, and after 12 rounds the disproportion rate is no lower.

These observations motivate a rethink of where learning signals for agent behavior belong. Current methods learn at the turns where the outcome changes, whereas over-defense is decided at turns where it does not, so the signal has to be located by behavior and placed where behavior diverges. Locating the signal by behavior also removes the per-turn Monte Carlo rollouts (Wang et al., 2024; Kazemnejad et al., 2025) that estimate a success probability constant at silent forks. We let the behavioral checker decide where to learn. It marks the first turn at which a successful trajectory departs from proportionate behavior, and the model, resampled from the same prefix, supplies the proportionate alternative. To teach the model to check as much as the task requires, we also pair silent forks at which submitting would skip a required check, constraining the other side of the required behavior. Our method, ForkDPO (fork-level DPO), applies preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) to both pair sets. On 48 test tasks from unseen repositories, it lowers the implicit-budget disproportion rate of a 4B model from 70.3% to 58.9% and, by removing repeated runs and extra checks, cuts the median run time from 143 to 90 seconds, whereas DPO with pairs at random turns leaves the rate at 67.7%.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • ❶

    Silent-Fork Diagnosis. We identify silent forks as the turns where over-defense begins in coding agents, from a 4B model to 4 frontier models, and show that outcome signals vanish while a checker in the trajectory reward reaches them only through fully proportionate trajectories.

  • ❷

    Rethinking Where to Learn. We show learning signals for agent behavior belong at the turns where behavior diverges, which a behavioral checker can locate and the outcome cannot. We instantiate this as ForkDPO, which learns from fork-level pairs on both sides of the required behavior, so that post-training shapes how agents act beyond whether they finish.

  • ❸

    Experimental Validation. On 48 test tasks from unseen repositories, signals at silent forks cut disproportion by 11.4 points and run time by 37%, which GRPO and DPO at random turns do not, and pairs on both sides of the required behavior are necessary.

2 Related Work

Over-defense and the cost of excess work. As coding agents take on longer tasks, how much work they spend has become a concern alongside whether they succeed. ParanoiaEval pairs repository tasks that differ only in the evidence ruling a defensive action out (Luo et al., 2026), trajectory analyses list tests rerun on unchanged patches among recurring inefficiencies (Hu et al., 2026), and evaluations expose edits to already-fixed code (Gloaguen et al., 2026), repairs larger than the minimal patch (Zhu et al., 2026), and reasoning in place of interaction (Cuadron et al., 2025). Remedies reward less work, with tool-call rewards that peak at the fewest calls still yielding a correct answer (Wang et al., 2025a), length penalties on correct responses (Arora and Zanette, 2025), and edit-distance rewards for code repair in the over-editing study. These works measure or price the amount of work without explaining why outcome-trained models keep doing it. Their remedies also push in one direction, so a reward for the least work that still passes counts a required check as excess as readily as a redundant one. We trace over-defense instead to silent forks, where outcome rewards carry no signal, and train there against both doing too much and skipping a required check.

Where learning signals are placed. Since outcome rewards are sparse, many methods concentrate the signal where the outcome is decided, starting with process supervision of intermediate steps (Lightman et al., 2024). Preference methods focus it on tokens (Zeng et al., 2024), on pivotal tokens that shift the probability of success (Abdin et al., 2024), or on the first erroneous step (Lai et al., 2024), much as RL can update only the high-entropy forking tokens without loss (Wang et al., 2025b). Agent RL assigns step-level credit through grouped states (Feng et al., 2025), privileged critics (Zhou et al., 2025), pivot turns with mixed outcomes (Yi et al., 2026), rollout-tree branches whose outcomes differ (Ji et al., 2026), or each tool call’s effect on answering correctly (Feng et al., 2026). Agent preference pairs contrast expert trajectories with failed explorations (Song et al., 2024) or expert steps with lower-scoring agent steps (Xiong et al., 2024). All of these give credit or form a pair only where outcomes differ or a step is wrong, so a silent fork, where every next action leads to the same outcome and no step is wrong, gets no weight by construction. In contrast, we locate such turns by behavior and pair two actions at the same state.

3 Preliminaries

Coding-agent trajectories. A task qq specifies a repository state and an instruction. A model πθ\pi_{\theta} interacts with a sandboxed repository and produces a trajectory τ=(s0,a0,o0,…,sT,aT)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},o_{0},\dots,s_{T},a_{T}), where sts_{t} is the interaction history, ata_{t} is a shell command or a submission, and oto_{t} is the observed output. A task oracle inspects the final repository and returns S⁡(τ)∈{0,1}S(\tau)\in\{0,1\}, the outcome of the run. Outcome-based post-training uses this outcome as a verifiable reward (Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025).

Behavioral checker. A checker CC replays the commands in τ\tau and tracks the task state, including which edits have landed and which required checks have run. For each action it decides whether the action is over-defensive, such as rerunning a passed target test, running tests outside the requested scope, or adding unrequested checks, and whether a submission skips a required check. We write propC​(at∣st)\mathrm{prop}_{C}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) when neither holds and propC​(τ)\mathrm{prop}_{C}(\tau) when it holds for every action in τ\tau. The checker also marks a run complete when it does what the instruction asks with every check that the instruction states.

Proportionate Behavior: For a coding task qq, a run should satisfy three conditions.
(1) Success. The run passes the oracle, S⁡(τ)=1{S(\tau)=1}. (2) Sufficiency. Every check that qq requires runs before submission. (3) Necessity. Every defensive action is one that qq requires. The oracle verifies (1), and the checker verifies (2) and (3), the two sides of the required behavior.

Explicit and implicit budgets. Each task comes in two arms. In the explicit-budget arm, the instruction states how much checking is required, such as running one named test once. In the implicit-budget arm, the instruction omits this and the agent must infer a proportionate amount from the task, much as reasoning models must decide how many tokens to spend on a problem (Han et al., 2025). We report the violation rate on explicit-budget tasks and the disproportion rate on implicit-budget tasks. Appendix B gives the checker’s rules, the thresholds of both rates, and its audits against blind annotation.

4 Silent Forks

Definition (Silent Fork).

A silent fork is a turn at which the agent’s next actions differ in proportionality while all of them lead to the same outcome. Formally, turn tt is a silent fork if its state sts_{t} satisfies

P(S=1∣st,a)=ct∀a∈suppπθ(⋅∣st),∃a+,a−∈suppπθ(⋅∣st):propC​(a+∣st)∧¬propC​(a−∣st).\begin{gathered}P(S=1\mid s_{t},a)=c_{t}\quad\forall a\in\operatorname{supp}\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\\ \exists\,a^{+},a^{-}\in\operatorname{supp}\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}):\\ \mathrm{prop}_{C}(a^{+}\mid s_{t})\wedge\neg\mathrm{prop}_{C}(a^{-}\mid s_{t}).\end{gathered} (1)

At an over-defense fork, the disproportionate action a−a^{-} breaks Necessity, and at a skipped-check fork, it breaks Sufficiency.

Setup. Like recent pipelines that synthesize executable software-engineering tasks (Yang et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2025), we generate 368 tasks from 34 Python and Go repositories with templates that read the repository’s own tests and constants, and keep a task when its target command passes and, for edit tasks, when the reference patch passes the oracle and a no-op patch fails it. We train on 318 tasks from 30 repositories and test on 48 tasks from 4 repositories unseen in training. The 4B model is Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) in mini-swe-agent (Yang et al., 2024), with samples served by vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). We examine its successful trajectories on training tasks and four frontier models, GPT-6.1-sol (OpenAI, 2026), Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026, Opus-5.5;), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026, DS-V4.1-Flash;), and GLM-5.3 (Z.ai, 2026), both at the 4B model’s forks and as end-to-end agents on the test tasks. Appendices C and D describe the tasks and both settings. Our key Observations are presented below.

4.1 Over-Defense Begins at Silent Forks

Obs.❶ Over-defense leaves the outcome unchanged. As shown in Figure 2.a, over-defensive runs pass the task oracle as often as the rest: 97.8% against 96.5% over the GRPO rollouts of the 4B model, and 98.0% against 97.1% on implicit-budget tasks, where over-defense is most frequent. Run end to end on our test tasks, the frontier models show the same pattern, with 98.8–100.0% against 100.0%. An outcome reward therefore never favors over-defense and cannot tell an over-defensive success from a proportionate one. The two differ in cost, as Table 1 shows. Compared with its own proportionate runs of the same task, the 4B model takes 1.50×\times as long when it over-defends under implicit budgets, and the frontier models take 1.46×\times as long. On the test tasks, the over-defensive runs that do fail are those whose repeated full-suite runs lead the 4B model to rewrite the test configuration or exhaust the time or step limit. Appendix E describes these runs.

Obs.❷ Over-defense begins at forks where neither branch changes the repository. At 316 of the 317 forks where a successful trajectory of the 4B model first becomes disproportionate, neither branch changes the repository: they run tests or checks, install test dependencies, or submit. Since the oracle inspects the repository and the disproportionate branch succeeded, both branches pass it. In the frontier runs of Table 2, the first disproportionate command leaves the repository unchanged in 89.3–100.0% of over-defensive runs.

Obs.❸ Frontier models split at the same forks. We give the 4B model’s fork prefixes to four frontier models and label each sampled next action with the same checker. Figure 2.b summarizes the labels. When the instruction states the budget, they rarely take the disproportionate branch, from 0.6% of samples for GPT-6.1-sol to 27.2% for GLM-5.3. When it does not, they take it in 81–91% of their decisive actions at full-suite forks, mostly with full-suite runs. At skipped-check forks, none of them submits early, so the split is specific to over-defense forks.

4.2 Existing Signals Miss Silent Forks

Two properties of silent forks explain why outcome rewards, outcome-located credit, and trajectory-level penalties miss them.

Proposition 1.

Let the reward be R⁡(τ)=S⁡(τ)R(\tau)=S(\tau) and let ss be the state at a silent fork. Then the contribution of ss to the policy gradient, ∑a∇θπθ​(a∣s)​Qπ​(s,a)\sum_{a}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\,Q^{\pi}(s,a), is zero, and any score of the form P⁡(S=1∣s,a)−P⁡(S=1∣s)P(S=1\mid s,a)-P(S=1\mid s) is zero for every aa in the support.

Proposition 2.

Suppose a successful trajectory passes mm silent forks and the model acts proportionately at fork ii with probability pip_{i}, independently across forks. Under R⁡(τ)=S⁡(τ)⋅𝟏​[propC​(τ)]R(\tau)=S(\tau)\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{prop}_{C}(\tau)], a group of GG rollouts has non-zero reward variance with probability 1−(1−ρ)G−ρG1-(1-\rho)^{G}-\rho^{G}, where ρ=∏i=1mpi\rho=\prod_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}.

Proposition 1 explains why outcome-located credit misses silent forks. Turn-level critics (Zhou et al., 2024) fare no better, since under R=SR=S the value they estimate is the same for every action there. Proposition 2 explains why a trajectory-level penalty helps little, as ρ\rho shrinks geometrically with mm, whereas a signal at the fork only needs pip_{i} to be non-negligible. Proofs are in Appendix F.

Obs.❹ A trajectory-level penalty leaves over-defense unchanged. We train with GRPO for 12 rounds under the reward S⁡(τ)⋅𝟏​[propC​(τ)]S(\tau)\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{prop}_{C}(\tau)], which penalizes over-defense explicitly, and Figure 3.a tracks the run. In 71% of implicit-budget groups every trajectory receives the same reward, so most groups contribute no gradient, and in 56% no trajectory is proportionate from start to finish. On implicit-budget test tasks, the disproportion rate stays within 57.3–64.6% over the 12 rounds, and the task-level bootstrap 95% CI of its change from round 0 to round 12 is [−2.1,+12.5][-2.1,+12.5] points. The penalty can punish over-defense in principle, but most groups offer no contrast to learn from, so the signal is too sparse to change behavior.

Obs.❺ Proportionate steps stay easy to sample as trajectories grow. As Proposition 2 predicts and Figure 3.b shows, groups with no proportionate trajectory become more frequent as trajectories grow longer, from 26% when the median trajectory has at most 4 commands to 74%, 67%, and 85% for 5–8, 9–15, and more than 15. At the fork itself, however, the alternative is a single step away, as 12 samples from the same prefix contain an action the checker accepts in 264 of 317 cases. The proportionate step is easy to sample, whereas a fully proportionate trajectory grows rare with length and a trajectory-level reward pays only for the latter, so the signal belongs at the fork itself.

5 Learning at Silent Forks

Following this finding, ForkDPO places the learning signal at the fork itself. It applies preference learning at the turns where behavior diverges and contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action at the same prefix, as Figure 4 shows.

5.1 Locating Silent Forks and Their Contrasts

Checker state. Replaying the commands a<ta_{<t} and outputs o<to_{<t}, the checker maintains a task state σt\sigma_{t} that records whether the requested edit has landed and how many effective runs of each required check have occurred. From σt\sigma_{t} it derives the checks still owed, ℛ⁡(σt)\mathcal{R}(\sigma_{t}), and the over-defensive actions, 𝒪⁡(σt)\mathcal{O}(\sigma_{t}). An action aa is proportionate, propC​(a∣st)\mathrm{prop}_{C}(a\mid s_{t}), when it is not over-defensive and does not submit while a check is owed,

a∉𝒪⁡(σt)∧(a≠asub∨ℛ⁡(σt)=∅).a\notin\mathcal{O}(\sigma_{t})\ \wedge\ \big(a\neq a^{\text{sub}}\vee\mathcal{R}(\sigma_{t})=\emptyset\big). (2)

Locating over-defense forks. For a successful trajectory, the over-defense fork is its first over-defensive turn,

t⋆=min⁡{t:at∈𝒪⁡(σt)}.t^{\star}=\min\{\,t:\ a_{t}\in\mathcal{O}(\sigma_{t})\,\}. (3)

This takes one replay of the trajectory and no per-turn Monte Carlo estimate of P⁡(S=1∣st,a)P(S=1\mid s_{t},a), which is the same for every action at a silent fork.

Same-prefix boundary action. We draw a(1),…,a(K)∼πθ(⋅∣st⋆)a^{(1)},\dots,a^{(K)}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t^{\star}}) and accept the first that lies on the boundary of the required behavior,

a+=a(k⋆),k⋆=min⁡{k:a(k)∈ℬ⁡(σt⋆)},a^{+}=a^{(k^{\star})},\qquad k^{\star}=\min\big\{k:\ a^{(k)}\in\mathcal{B}(\sigma_{t^{\star}})\big\}, (4)

where ℬ⁡(σ)={asub}\mathcal{B}(\sigma)=\{a^{\text{sub}}\} if ℛ⁡(σ)=∅\mathcal{R}(\sigma)=\emptyset and ℬ⁡(σ)=ℛ⁡(σ)\mathcal{B}(\sigma)=\mathcal{R}(\sigma) otherwise, so the boundary action is to submit once the required checks have run and otherwise run the owed check once. The rejected action is the agent’s own, a−=at⋆a^{-}=a_{t^{\star}}. The accepted sample and the agent’s own action come from the same model at the same state, so the pair isolates the decision and stays on-policy, which helps preference fine-tuning (Tajwar et al., 2024) and avoids the squeezing effect that Ren and Sutherland (2025) observe for off-policy DPO. The chosen action a+a^{+} is also the least behavior that still suffices, so it cannot be another form of extra work. If no sample is accepted, we take the submission turn of a proportionate trajectory for the task.

Skipped-check forks. Proportionate trajectories supply pairs for Sufficiency, at the turn of the first required check,

tr=min⁡{t:at∈ℛ⁡(σt)},(a+,a−)=(atr,asub),t_{r}=\min\{t:a_{t}\in\mathcal{R}(\sigma_{t})\},\;\;(a^{+},a^{-})=(a_{t_{r}},a^{\text{sub}}), (5)

where the premature submission asuba^{\text{sub}} is taken from another trajectory for the same task. Like an over-defense fork, this turn is silent once the prefix meets what the oracle requires, and only the checker separates the two actions. These pairs keep Sufficiency in place while over-defense pairs teach Necessity.

5.2 Fork-Level Objective and Training

Let 𝒟over\mathcal{D}_{\text{over}} and 𝒟skip\mathcal{D}_{\text{skip}} denote the over-defense pairs and the skipped-check pairs. ForkDPO minimizes

ℒfork​(θ)=𝔼𝒟over​[ℓθ]+λ​𝔼𝒟skip​[ℓθ],\mathcal{L}_{\text{fork}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{over}}}\big[\ell_{\theta}\big]+\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{skip}}}\big[\ell_{\theta}\big], (6)

where λ\lambda weights the skipped-check side, set to |𝒟skip|/|𝒟over||\mathcal{D}_{\text{skip}}|/|\mathcal{D}_{\text{over}}| so that every pair counts equally, and ℓθ\ell_{\theta} is the DPO loss (Rafailov et al., 2023). With the implicit reward hθ​(s,a)=β​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)πref​(a∣s)h_{\theta}(s,a)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a\mid s)} against the base model πref\pi_{\text{ref}},

ℓθ​(s,a+,a−)=log⁡(1+ehθ​(s,a−)−hθ​(s,a+)).\ell_{\theta}(s,a^{+},a^{-})=\log\big(1+e^{\,h_{\theta}(s,a^{-})-h_{\theta}(s,a^{+})}\big). (7)

Under the token-level view of DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024), the implicit reward is an optimal advantage, hθ​(s,a)=Q∗​(s,a)−V∗​(s)h_{\theta}(s,a)=Q^{*}(s,a)-V^{*}(s), so a pair that shares its prefix raises the optimal-advantage gap A∗​(st⋆,a+)−A∗​(st⋆,a−)A^{*}(s_{t^{\star}},a^{+})-A^{*}(s_{t^{\star}},a^{-}) at the fork. ForkDPO therefore supplies a checker-defined advantage at exactly the states where Proposition 1 shows the outcome advantage to vanish.

In practice, the pairs are mined once from successful runs of the base model on the training tasks, and Eq. (6) is optimized offline. The checker enters only when the pairs are built, so the trained model runs without it at the cost of the base model. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

6 Experiments

We test whether pairs at silent forks reduce over-defense on unseen repositories, whether both sides are needed, and whether their placement matters.

6.1 Experimental Setup

Training and evaluation. ForkDPO and the GRPO baseline train LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) on the 318 training tasks, ForkDPO with TRL (von Werra et al., 2020). Evaluation samples k=8k=8 explicit-budget and k=4k=4 implicit-budget runs per test task at temperature 1.0. Guardrail tasks, whose correct behavior is to delete a file or edit without guards, check that training adds no defensive code. Appendix H gives the training configuration and the evaluation protocol.

Baselines. We compare ForkDPO with the base model, with GRPO under the reward S⁡(τ)⋅𝟏​[propC​(τ)]S(\tau)\cdot\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{prop}_{C}(\tau)], and with DPO on pairs placed at random turns, which keeps the trajectories, pair count, skipped-check forks, acceptance rule, and training schedule of ForkDPO and moves each over-defense pair to a turn drawn uniformly from its trajectory. The explicit-budget arm, which states the required checking, serves as the instruction-only control, and the frontier models we examined as references.

Metrics and checker reliability. We report the violation rate on explicit-budget tasks and the disproportion rate on implicit-budget tasks, the latter split into full-suite runs and other forms, as well as completion, the oracle pass rate, and median wall-clock time. Against two rounds of blind annotation on 177 and 117 runs, the checker reaches precision/recall of at least 0.93/0.92 for over-defense and 0.89/0.94 for completion, and agrees with blind annotation on 92 of 96 single actions at forks.

6.2 Results

Signals at silent forks reduce over-defense on unseen repositories. As shown in Table 3, ForkDPO lowers implicit-budget disproportion from 70.3% to 58.9%, raises completion from 82.8% to 85.9%, and cuts the median run from 143 to 90 seconds. Its implicit-budget disproportion is also lower than that of the four frontier models, which range from 64.0% to 97.9%. The task-level bootstrap 95% CI of the disproportion change is [−19.8,−3.6][-19.8,-3.6] points. Python run tasks change most, from 89.3% to 68.8%, with 11 tasks improving and none worsening, and repeated target runs on Go explicit-budget tasks fall from 12.5% to 0%, while 1.6% of explicit-budget runs submit without the check.

Both sides of the required behavior are needed. As shown in Table 4, over-defense pairs alone, with λ=0\lambda=0, teach Necessity at the cost of Sufficiency: up to 11.9% of test runs submit without the required check, completion on training-distribution tasks falls from 99% to 70%, and guardrail tasks acquire new guard code. Mixing in skipped-check pairs at equal weight per pair removes every submit-only run and restores completion on every set, while median time stays 36–50% below the base.

The reduction sits in the behaviors the forks contrast. In Figure 5.a, disproportion without a full-suite run, mostly repeated runs and extra checks, falls from 16.7% to 6.3%, so the gain does not rest on the full-suite rule, whereas full-suite runs stay at 53.6% and 52.6%. Every remaining violation on Python run tasks under implicit budgets is a full-suite run. Fewer reruns and checks account for the time saved, which Figure 5.b shows falling from 930 to 330 seconds per Python run task.

Pairs away from the fork teach little. At random turns, DPO leaves disproportion at 67.7% and other disproportion at 14.6%, against 58.9% and 6.3% for ForkDPO, while full-suite runs stay at 51–54% under every method, so the methods differ in the behaviors the pairs contrast. A trajectory has one over-defense fork, its first disproportionate turn, and Figure 6 shows that these forks come early, with the median one after two actions and 66% after at most two. A turn drawn uniformly from the trajectory therefore rarely lands on the fork, and only 21.3% of the random-turn pairs land on a disproportionate action.

Placement decides success. GRPO puts the same checker into its reward and moves neither rate across 12 rounds, going from 59.4% to 64.6% after 6,883 rollouts and 9.5 hours of updates, whereas ForkDPO learns from 488 pairs in 244 updates and under one hour, as Table 5 shows. The three methods share the checker and differ in where its judgment enters training, over whole trajectories, at random turns, or at silent forks. Figure 7 shows that the reduction follows the share of the signal placed at violating forks, about a fifth of the reduction under ForkDPO at random turns and none over whole trajectories. The ordering matches Proposition 2, since a trajectory-level reward pays only for trajectories that are proportionate at every fork and then spreads that payment over every turn of the rollout, whereas a fork pair needs a single proportionate step and places its judgment on the turn where behavior diverges. Where a behavioral signal is placed, more than how much training it receives, decides whether the model learns it.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we show that over-defense in coding agents begins at silent forks, the turns where every next action leads to the same outcome. Outcome rewards, outcome-located credit, and trajectory-level penalties cannot reach these turns, and frontier models split there as a 4B model does. Learning from pairs placed there and constrained on both sides, ForkDPO reduces over-defense and run time on unseen repositories more than GRPO and DPO at random turns. We believe that placing learning signals where behavior diverges offers a general recipe for shaping how agents act beyond whether they finish, from checks to tool calls.

Limitations

We note several limitations of our work:

  • ➠

    Training frontier models is beyond our budget, as most of them do not release their weights and the open ones are too large for our compute. We therefore diagnose frontier models and train a single 4B model, and the size of the effect may differ for larger models. All tasks come from open-source Python and Go repositories.

  • ➠

    All runs use a minimal agent harness with a single bash tool and no dedicated tools for testing, editing, or planning. This keeps every choice at a fork with the model itself and also places our setting at some distance from deployed agents, where richer tools or pipelines that fix the order of localization, repair, and patch validation (Xia et al., 2025) may present different forks.

  • ➠

    The checker is written as rules, so every label is reproducible and can be audited against blind annotation, while its coverage bounds what can be taught. Behavior that no pair covers, such as out-of-scope edits on explicit-budget tasks, can also increase (Zhong et al., 2026).

  • ➠

    We study tasks whose proportionate amount of checking can be decided from the instruction and the repository, so that proportionate behavior has an objective criterion. Behaviors whose appropriate amount depends on unstated user preferences or on the cost of a failure in deployment are outside this scope.

  • ➠

    A fork pair contrasts two actions at one state, so over-defense that only emerges from a sequence of individually proportionate actions has no single turn at which it can be located.

Contents of Appendix

Appendix A Notation

Table 6 collects the symbols used in the main text and in this appendix, with the value each takes in our experiments.

Appendix B Checker Rules and Audit

The checker replays a run’s commands and outputs, tracks the task state, and labels completion and over-defense with the fixed rules of Table 7.

B.1 Effective Runs, Completion, and Thresholds

The rules below define what counts as a run and when a task is done.

What counts as a run. The checker counts test runs as follows:

  • •

    An effective run is a test command that printed results, such as N passed, N failed, N errors, or Go ok/FAIL/PASS after ANSI codes are stripped, and that shows no hard-failure signature, such as errors during collection, no tests ran, INTERNALERROR, usage: pytest, file or directory not found, command not found, build failed, cannot find package, or no Go files.

  • •

    A run redirected with > file or | tee file counts if it exits with code 0 or 1. Merging streams with 2>&1 alone does not count as redirection.

  • •

    A failed run followed by an environment fix, such as pip install, uv sync, uv add, apt-get, or go mod download, does not count, and the fix is never over-defense.

  • •

    A test command counts only in command position, after echo and printf segments are removed.

  • •

    Loops and chains count once per execution, with for i in 1 2 3, {1..5}, seq, and range(n) expanded.

  • •

    On edit-and-verify tasks, runs count from the last edit of the target file.

When a task is done. Table 8 gives the completion condition and the run limit of each task type. A submit-only run submits without any command other than reads. An environment-blocked run lands the edit and attempts the target without an effective run.

B.2 Rules

The explicit-budget arm flags anything beyond the stated check, whereas the implicit-budget arm has no target and flags only disproportion.

B.3 Audit Protocol and Agreement

Two annotation experts from the author team label every audited run. They are distinct from the team members who wrote the checker. Each run is exported to a sheet with the instruction, the numbered commands with exit codes and output tails, the changed files, the patch, and the final report, without any checker verdict. The experts review each sheet independently, without seeing each other’s labels, and record completion, every action beyond the required checking with its form and command numbers, and unsupported claims in the final report. They then compare their records and discuss every disagreement until they reach a consensus, and only consensus labels serve as references. Round 1 samples 177 of the 618 explicit-budget Python runs of the base model, stratified by task type and checker verdict, which gives 99 run and 78 edit-and-verify runs. Round 2 samples 117 runs stratified by model, arm, language, and verdict. Table 9 summarizes both rounds, and Table 10 gives the agreement of the checker with the consensus labels.

Annotation rules. The experts apply the written rules of Table 7 to observable actions. An action counts as over-defense when it tests, checks, or guards beyond what the instruction requires, such as rerunning a passed target, running tests outside the requested scope, or adding an unrequested check. Reading the repository, the required target run, a rerun after an intervening edit, a final inspection of the diff, and steps the environment requires stay within the baseline. Task failure and unsupported claims in the final report are recorded separately and do not by themselves count as over-defense.

B.4 Examples of Each Violation Type

B.5 Labeling Single Actions at Forks

To label one proposed action, we replay the prefix with the state machine that located the fork, append the action as if it produced results, and apply the rules above with the checker’s own functions. Table 11 lists the resulting labels. A text reply without a tool call counts as a submission, unless it ends with a command in the prefix’s text format, which then counts as that command. Read-only commands are masked first, so grep -E "pytest" is not a test run. A blind annotation of 96 sampled actions agrees with these labels on 92.

Appendix C Task Construction

Tasks are generated from each repository’s own tests and constants, gated inside the repository’s image, and split by repository.

C.1 Generators and Arms

Table 12 lists the four generators that produce the 368 tasks. Run tasks (P1) name a test file (Python) or a package with _test.go files (Go). Edit-and-verify tasks (P4) are mined from module-level string lists (Python) and []string slices (Go). The agent appends zz_extra_entry and runs the test matched to the module, and the oracle requires the entry and a passing test. Delete tasks (P2) remove an unreferenced script, and parameter tasks (P3), written with a language model, add an optional parameter to an internal function. In both, correct behavior adds no defensive code, so they are guardrails.

For P1 and P4 the two arms differ only in the instruction. Arm B omits the command of single-run tasks, replaces the count of repeated-run tasks with “a few times”, and drops the verification sentence of P4. For P2, arm A adds that no deprecation note is needed. For P3, the instructions are identical and arm B adds a code comment that the parameter comes from user configuration.

C.2 Gates and Splits

A task is kept only if, inside its image, the target command passes, a no-op patch fails the oracle, and the reference patch passes it. The oracle of a run task requires an unchanged tree, so there the gate checks the target command alone. The four test repositories, garak, troposphere, feast, and restic, contribute no training task. Their 48 run and edit-and-verify tasks form the main evaluation, and their two delete tasks join the guardrails. Tables 13–14 give the counts.

C.3 Agent Harness

The model runs in mini-swe-agent, and each command runs through docker exec in a fresh subshell of the task’s container. A run ends at submission, after 50 steps, or at a time limit. Each call generates with thinking on and top-pp 0.95, and the instance message is the instruction alone.

Appendix D Frontier Diagnosis

We diagnose four frontier models in two settings, at the 4B model’s fork prefixes, where one next action is sampled and labeled, and end to end as coding agents on our test tasks.

D.1 Fork Probe

Each 4B prefix is converted into a tool-calling conversation with a single bash tool. Every executed command becomes an assistant tool call, its observation the tool result (exit code <rc> and the output), reasoning text stays in the assistant message, and the instruction and the harness’s format reminders stay user messages. Every fork is sent to every model four times as independent requests with reasoning effort high and the maximum output length each provider allows.

Cost. Requests are charged at list prices per million input, cached, cache-write, and output tokens (DS-V4.1-Flash 0.30/0.006/0.30/1.20, GLM-5.3 1.40/0.26/1.40/4.40, Opus-5.5 4.00/0.20/5.00/20.0, GPT-6.1-sol 2.00/0.10/2.50/10.0 US$). The fork probe costs US$19.98.

Results. Table 15 and Figure 8 give the labels at all forks. Inspection covers reading files, checking tool versions, collecting tests without running them, environment fixes, and edits.

Table 16 gives their sub-kinds.

D.2 Frontier Models End to End on Our Tasks

The fork probe fixes the prefix to the 4B model’s own history. To measure over-defense without a fixed prefix, the same four models run at reasoning effort high as end-to-end coding agents on the 48 test run and edit-and-verify tasks, with 8 runs per task in the explicit-budget arm and 4 in the implicit-budget arm, as for the 4B models. They call the single bash tool with the system prompt of the fork probe, receive the instruction as the user message, and run in the task’s Docker image with 50 steps. The final checker labels the executed commands with the run-level rules of arm A in the explicit arm and the rules of arm B in the implicit arm, and the oracle is recorded for every run. The first violation is the index of the first command the checker flags, divided by the number of commands. Table 17 reports the results next to those of the 4B models.

Appendix E Over-Defensive Runs That Fail

On the test tasks, the implicit-budget over-defensive runs of the base model that fail the oracle are feast run tasks that run the full suite two to seventeen times. Most of them then write a pytest configuration file into the repository, which a run task must leave unchanged, and some end at the time or step limit. On training tasks the rates are close, with 98.0% of implicit-budget over-defensive rollouts passing against 97.1% of the others.

Appendix G Fork Mining and Pair Statistics

Fork pairs are mined from the base model’s own runs on training tasks in the steps below, and the 507 pairs come from 258 tasks in 30 repositories.

  • •

    Runs. 4,660 base-policy runs at temperature 1.0 over 157.7 agent hours, with k=8k=8 in the explicit arm, k=2k=2–88 in the implicit arm, and k=16k=16 more explicit runs on the 64 tasks with an explicit violation.

  • •

    Over-defense fork. The first turn whose command the checker’s state machine flags, in runs whose oracle passes.

  • •

    Rejected action a−a^{-}. That turn, with its reasoning restored.

  • •

    Resampling. K=12K=12 continuations from the same prefix at temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95, and top-kk 20, with thinking on and up to 4,000 tokens.

  • •

    Chosen action a+a^{+}. The first boundary continuation, which submits if the required runs are complete and otherwise runs the target once, and extra checks and full-suite commands are rejected. If none is accepted, a+a^{+} is a submission turn from a proportionate run of the task.

  • •

    Skipped check. The state before the first target run of a clean, completed run, where a+a^{+} is that run and a−a^{-} a submission from another run of the task.

  • •

    Mixing. 326 over-defense pairs, 321 after deduplication by run and turn, and 317 after a cap of four per task and arm. The 190 skipped-check pairs are added at 0.6×0.6\times, edit-and-verify first.

  • •

    Length filter. Prompts up to 5,000 tokens and longer responses up to 1,500 tokens, which keeps 488 of the 507 pairs.

G.1 Composition of the Pair Set

Table 18 breaks the 507 pairs down by kind.

G.2 Why the Forks Are Silent

The first condition of the silent-fork definition requires every next action to lead to the same outcome. At an over-defense fork the trajectory that took the disproportionate branch succeeded (S=1S=1), so the prefix already meets what the oracle requires. A continuation that leaves the repository as it is keeps this outcome, since the oracle inspects the repository. At 316 of the 317 over-defense forks neither action changes it, as Table 19 shows. The exception reruns the target after editing a test file with sed -i (gev2-SDV-dayz-required-relationship-keys). The turn of the first required check is silent for the same reason once the prefix meets what the oracle requires, since a premature submission leaves the repository as the check would. Skipped-check pairs placed there keep Sufficiency in place.

Appendix H Training Details

This section gives the configuration of ForkDPO and its training curve, GRPO, the DPO baseline at random turns, and the evaluation protocol.

H.1 ForkDPO

ForkDPO trains a LoRA adapter with the DPO loss, both sides mixed at equal weight per pair, against the base model as reference with precomputed log-probabilities, and the adapter is merged into the base weights and served with vLLM. Table 20 lists its configuration next to the two pilot runs of the earlier round.

H.2 Training Curve

Figure 9 plots the logged loss, reward margin, and preference accuracy of the three runs. ForkDPO fits its pairs within the first epoch, with a mean loss of 0.087 and an accuracy of 0.96 over steps 62–122 and 0.010 and 1.00 afterwards, whereas the two-sided pilot does not saturate and ends with a margin of 1.51.

H.3 GRPO

GRPO runs 12 rounds with the configuration of Table 21.

Table 22 and Figure 10 trace every round. Explicit-budget Python run tasks are saturated from the first round, so nearly all gradient comes from the implicit arm, whose Python run tasks stay between 0.15 and 0.42 without a trend. Only 301 of 1,136 groups carry a signal. As Table 23 shows, most implicit groups contain no proportionate trajectory, and more so as trajectories grow longer.

A round takes 1.8–2.5 hours (sampling 60–105 minutes, update 30–75 minutes), and sampling is bound by containers and CPUs. Updates take 9.5 hours over the 12 rounds and the run about 26 GPU hours in total.

H.4 DPO at Random Turns

The control is identical to ForkDPO except that each over-defense pair is moved to a turn drawn uniformly from the same trajectory, where the alternative is resampled under the same acceptance rule. Skipped-check pairs, length filter, and schedule are unchanged. After the length filter, 488 pairs remain, of which the 300 over-defense pairs are moved. The rejected action is a violation under the final checker in 64 of the moved pairs, and 29 of the drawn turns coincide with the over-defense fork.

H.5 Evaluation Protocol

All policies run on the 48 test run and edit-and-verify tasks with the same harness at temperature 1.0: k=8k=8 explicit and k=4k=4 implicit runs per task for the base model, ForkDPO, and DPO, and k=4k=4 and k=2k=2 for the GRPO checkpoints of rounds 0, 4, 8, and 12. Explicit-budget runs take about a minute and rarely violate the budget, so this arm gets more runs per task than the implicit arm, whose runs take two to five minutes. Every run is labeled by the final checker. Confidence intervals resample the 48 tasks with replacement 10,000 times (seed 0), recompute the rate difference over all runs of the resampled tasks, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

Appendix K Compute and Cost

Agent runs of the 4B model are bound by Docker containers and CPUs. Each run occupies one container, an explicit-budget run takes about a minute and an implicit-budget run two to five minutes, and runs proceed in parallel against vLLM servers. Table 29 lists the local compute of each stage.

Fork resampling draws continuations of up to 4,000 tokens, and 264 of the 317 final pairs use a resample. GRPO serves the model on three GPUs and shares a fourth between a serving replica and the update. A round takes 1.8–2.5 hours. Agent hours sum the wall-clock time of agent runs. The software is mini-swe-agent 2.4.6, vLLM 0.26, TRL 1.13, and PEFT 0.20 (Mangrulkar et al., 2022).

The figure icons come from OpenMoji (HfG Schwäbisch Gmünd, 2019) under CC BY-SA 4.0 and Fluent Emoji (Microsoft, 2022) under MIT.
